levels.title: Level 1: Core Entity Definition & Encapsulation
levels.description: Isolate leaf domain objects, control state tracking metrics, and enforce strict structural visibility rules based on Domain-Driven Design principles.

questions.text: In a Parking Lot system, which core domain object represents a customer's immutable proof of entry and acts as a central 'Value Object' tracking temporal lifecycle bounds?
choices: ParkingTicket
DatabaseLoggerService
TicketIdString
questions.explanation: A ParkingTicket is a first-class Domain Entity. Unlike stateless utility services or primitive strings, it possesses a continuous temporal lifecycle, domain-specific behavior, and a distinct identity tracked via a unique identifier.

questions.text: The entry timestamp 'issuedAt' must be globally readable for fee calculation but strictly protected against post-issuance mutations (tampering). Which visibility and access strategy guarantees this invariant?
choices: + LocalDateTime issuedAt (Public field, directly accessed)
- LocalDateTime issuedAt (Private field with getter, no setter)
# LocalDateTime issuedAt (Protected field, allowing subclass mutations)
questions.correct_answer: - LocalDateTime issuedAt (Private field with getter, no setter)
questions.explanation: Private visibility (-) combined with an explicit accessor (getter) and the omission of a mutator (setter) ensures runtime immutability, preventing unauthorized state modification after object instantiation.

questions.text: The parking ticket shifts through specific states (ACTIVE, PAID, LOST). What is the safest architectural structure to prevent invalid state injections (like 'PENDNG' instead of 'PENDING') into our domain framework?
choices: A flexible String variable named 'status'
An integer status code variable (e.g., 0, 1, 2) mapped in documentation
A dedicated TicketStatus Enumeration
questions.explanation: Enums enforce compile-time type safety. They constrain the domain state space to an explicit pool of valid options, wiping out systemic typo errors, integer misinterpretations, and invalid state transitions.

questions.text: Link your newly created TicketStatus enumeration to the ParkingTicket class. What relationship accurately characterizes this structural connection?
choices: ParkingTicket inherits from TicketStatus (Generalization)
ParkingTicket holds a directional association to TicketStatus (Association)
TicketStatus contains a list of ParkingTickets (Composition)
questions.correct_answer: ParkingTicket holds a directional association to TicketStatus (Association)
questions.explanation: A ParkingTicket has an attribute containing a TicketStatus value. This represents a directed structural association where the ticket points to its current state definition.

levels.title: Level 2: Structural Relations & Multiplicity Mapping
levels.description: Establish multi-element containment boundaries, differentiate between Aggregation and Composition, and introduce polymorphic domain foundations.

questions.text: A ParkingFloor contains multiple ParkingSlots. If a ParkingFloor is structurally demolished, its corresponding ParkingSlots cease to exist. How is this strictly enforced in UML?
choices: Composition (Filled black diamond from ParkingFloor to ParkingSlot)
Aggregation (Hollow diamond from ParkingFloor to ParkingSlot)
Realization (Dotted line with hollow triangle)
questions.correct_answer: Composition (Filled black diamond from ParkingFloor to ParkingSlot)
questions.explanation: Composition (filled diamond) models a 'whole-part' relationship with strict lifecycle dependency. Since slots are physically bound to the floor, they cannot exist independently if the floor is destroyed.

questions.text: When a Vehicle parks in a ParkingSlot, the slot holds a reference to the vehicle. However, when the vehicle leaves, the slot remains. What relationship defines this temporary containment?
choices: Composition
Aggregation
Generalization
questions.explanation: Aggregation (hollow diamond) represents a 'has-a' relationship where the child (Vehicle) can exist independently of the parent (ParkingSlot). The slot does not own the vehicle's lifecycle.

questions.text: Our system must support Cars, Trucks, and Motorcycles. Each requires a different parking spot size. How should we structurally model this to allow dynamic size resolution at runtime?
choices: Create separate unrelated classes for Car, Truck, and Motorcycle.
Make Vehicle an abstract class with an abstract method getRequiredSpotType(), implemented by concrete subclasses.
Add a 'String type' variable to Vehicle and use an if-else chain in the parking assignment logic.
questions.correct_answer: Make Vehicle an abstract class with an abstract method getRequiredSpotType(), implemented by concrete subclasses.
questions.explanation: Using an abstract class and polymorphic methods avoids Open-Closed Principle violations. New vehicle types can be added seamlessly by creating new subclasses without modifying existing assignment logic.

levels.title: Level 3: Interface Behaviors & Design Patterns
levels.description: Utilize Gang of Four (GoF) design patterns to implement dynamic behaviors, decoupled interactions, and robust method signatures.

questions.text: The lot requires dynamic pricing models (Hourly, Flat Rate, Special Event) that can be swapped at runtime. Which behavioral design pattern is best suited for this?
choices: The Singleton Pattern
The Strategy Pattern
The Decorator Pattern
questions.explanation: The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms (pricing models), encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. This lets the fee calculation vary independently from the parking lot orchestrator.

questions.text: Looking at the PricingStrategy interface, why is passing the entire `ParkingTicket` object preferable to passing primitive values like `double hours` and `String vehicleType`?
choices: It minimizes memory allocation by avoiding primitive wrappers.
It improves flexibility; if a future pricing strategy requires new ticket data (e.g., entry gate ID), the interface signature doesn't need to break.
It forces tight coupling, which is desired in domain-driven design.
questions.correct_answer: It improves flexibility; if a future pricing strategy requires new ticket data (e.g., entry gate ID), the interface signature doesn't need to break.
questions.explanation: Passing an aggregate context object (the ticket) makes the method signature resilient to future changes (Open-Closed Principle), preventing a cascading interface modification if new parameters are needed.

questions.text: When a ParkingFloor becomes completely full, an electronic DisplayBoard at the entrance must update immediately. How should the ParkingFloor notify the DisplayBoard while remaining loosely coupled?
choices: The ParkingFloor should directly instantiate and call DisplayBoard.update().
Run a continuous while-loop thread inside DisplayBoard querying the floor's status.
Implement the Observer Pattern: the Floor acts as a Subject, notifying a generic Observer interface implemented by the DisplayBoard.
questions.correct_answer: Implement the Observer Pattern: the Floor acts as a Subject, notifying a generic Observer interface implemented by the DisplayBoard.
questions.explanation: The Observer Pattern allows the Subject (ParkingFloor) to broadcast state changes to multiple listeners (DisplayBoards, mobile apps) without depending on their concrete implementations.

levels.title: Level 4: System Orchestration & Concurrency
levels.description: Design the main entry point (Facade), manage structural orchestration, and handle thread-safe systemic operations.

questions.text: We need a central orchestrator class to handle external requests (entry, exit) and coordinate internal subsystems (floors, checkout). What architectural pattern best fits this single point of interaction?
choices: The Builder Pattern
The Facade Pattern (often combined with Singleton)
The Proxy Pattern
questions.correct_answer: The Facade Pattern (often combined with Singleton)
questions.explanation: A Facade provides a simplified, high-level interface to a complex subsystem. A central 'ParkingLotController' acts as a Facade, hiding the complexity of slot assignment, ticket generation, and fee calculation from the client.

questions.text: The ParkingLotController manages physical infrastructure. A large lot will have multiple EntryPanels and ExitPanels operating simultaneously. How is this mapped structurally?
choices: Controller has exactly one EntryPanel and one ExitPanel (1 to 1).
Controller aggregates multiple EntryPanels and ExitPanels (1 to Many).
EntryPanels and ExitPanels inherit from the Controller.
questions.correct_answer: Controller aggregates multiple EntryPanels and ExitPanels (1 to Many).
questions.explanation: A robust system supports high throughput by deploying multiple entry/exit gates, all reporting to the central controller. A '1 to *' mapping is required.

questions.text: When two cars arrive at different EntryPanels at the exact same millisecond, they might be assigned the last available ParkingSlot. How should the controller's `assignSlot()` method signature or design account for this?
choices: It must return void and use optimistic UI updates.
It should be designed as a thread-safe atomic operation (e.g., using synchronized blocks or concurrent locks on the slot pool) before returning the assigned ParkingSlot.
It should pass the Vehicle object directly to the database without validation.
questions.correct_answer: It should be designed as a thread-safe atomic operation (e.g., using synchronized blocks or concurrent locks on the slot pool) before returning the assigned ParkingSlot.
questions.explanation: In distributed or multi-threaded LLD systems, managing shared resources (available slots) requires mutual exclusion (locking) to prevent race conditions and overbooking.
